title: The lift (Story of a Soul)
hookLine: Thérèse, too small to climb the stairs of perfection, looks for a lift: Jesus' arms
tomorrow: what do you do when you want every calling at once?

lines: A GRAIN OF SAND BY A MOUNTAIN.
cards: The feed is full of climbs: the internship, the personal best, the acceptance letter, each one another step up. A young nun in a French convent is writing down how that feels.
Next to the saints, Thérèse says, she's a grain of sand beside a mountain whose peak is lost in the clouds. The stairs of perfection are long and rough, and she's too small to climb them.
Anyone else might put the pen down there. She goes looking for another way up.

teach.h: LIFTS IN THE HOUSES OF THE RICH.
teach.b: She finds it in something new in her own day. In the houses of the rich, she writes, there are now lifts, elevators that carry you up without the stairs.
She wants one: a lift to raise her to Jesus, since she's too little to climb the rough stairway of perfection. So she searches scripture, and finds two lines.
The first, from Proverbs, is wisdom calling out: whoever is a little one, let him come to me. That's how her Latin Bible reads it.
Here's the detail to tell a friend: the King James reads the same verse differently, “Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither.”
The second is from Isaiah, where God speaks like a mother: “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you.”

teach.h: CARRIED, AND ROCKED ON THE KNEES.
teach.b: Isaiah says the little ones will be carried, and rocked on the knees. That's her answer. The lift is the arms of Jesus.
She doesn't need to grow strong enough to climb.
She needs to stay little, even to become littler, and let herself be carried. It's an odd ambition. She still wants to be a saint; she says so.
But her way runs through smallness, and up only because someone else lifts. She calls it a little way, and it's honest about what she can't do. No pretending the stairs are short.

how: Catholics honor Thérèse of Lisieux as a saint, and Christians of other churches read Story of a Soul too; her little way is taught as trusting God like a small child.

o: Thérèse's picture: carried up in Jesus' arms, not climbing
a ladder of virtues that monks climb one rung at a time
the moment a saint is raised to the altar by the pope

games.q: the way up — tap the pairs.
p: whoso is simple, let him turn in
as one whom his mother comforteth

s: Thérèse's little way means not wanting to be a saint
she still wants to be a saint. her way up runs through smallness.
her picture comes from the new lifts in rich people's houses
she asks for one of her own: a lift to raise her to Jesus.
the King James and Thérèse's Latin Bible read Proverbs 9:4 the same
her Latin says little one; the King James says whoso is simple.

games.q: a friend says she's "not good enough to pray" after a rough year, so she's quitting until she's better. what fits Thérèse's lift?
o: get better first; come back once you can climb on your own.
you don't have to be strong enough. stay little, and let yourself be carried.
if you're not good enough, holiness probably isn't for you.
games.why: Thérèse was too small for the stairs and didn't pretend otherwise. she asked to be carried, and called that her little way.

practice: Let whatever is under you take your full weight: the chair, the floor, the bed. Loosen your shoulders, your jaw, your hands, and stop holding yourself up.
Isaiah's picture can rest with you there: carried, comforted the way a mother comforts a child.

wordCard.voice: The lift. Thérèse's picture: too small for the stairs, she's carried up in the arms of Jesus.

orig.note: Latin for 'little one', the word in the Proverbs verse as Thérèse's Latin Bible read it.

carryVoice: The line to keep: his arms are the lift. She didn't get strong; she got carried. Until tomorrow.
